B243: A Modern Way to Eat is a vegetarian cookbook by Anna Jones, a London food writer and former Jamie Oliver team member. It collects more than 150 recipes built around vegetables, grains, and pulses, organized by meal and by the way people cook day to day.
B290: Canal House Cooks Every Day is a seasonal cookbook from Melissa Hamilton and Christopher Hirsheimer, the pair behind the Canal House series. It gathers simple recipes, photographs, and notes from their studio kitchen in Lambertville, New Jersey, arranged by month of the year.
B244: Dinner: Changing the Game is a cookbook by New York Times food writer Melissa Clark. It offers weeknight recipes for home cooks, with a focus on quick preparation, flexible ingredients, and dishes that range from simple suppers to meals for guests.
B249: From the Oven to the Table is a cookbook by the British food writer Diana Henry. It presents simple dishes cooked in a single roasting pan, tray, or casserole, with chapters on roasts, bakes, and puddings and an emphasis on minimal washing up.
B261: Healing Mushrooms is a guide by Tero Isokauppila, a Finnish founder of a functional mushroom company. It covers varieties such as reishi, chaga, and cordyceps, summarizes their traditional and modern uses, and includes recipes for adding them to drinks and meals.
B192: Homebrewed Vinegar is a how-to guide by fermentation author Kirsten K. Shockey. It explains how to make vinegar from fruit, grains, vegetables, and other ingredients at home, and it includes recipes for using the finished vinegars in cooking and drinks.
B242: Lucky Peach: 101 Easy Asian Recipes collects quick dishes from the food magazine Lucky Peach, written with David Chang's Momofuku circle. Peter Meehan and the editors present recipes drawing on Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cooking, aimed at cooks working with a modest pantry.
B239: Soups, Salads, Sandwiches is a cookbook by Matty Matheson, a Canadian chef and television personality. It presents recipes for the three title categories in his hearty, informal style, ranging from classic comfort dishes to restaurant-influenced creations.
B294: The Cooking of the Eastern Mediterranean is a cookbook by Paula Wolfert, the American writer known for her work on Mediterranean food. It gathers 215 recipes from countries such as Greece, Turkey, Lebanon, and Syria, with notes on ingredients, techniques, and regional traditions.
B246: The New York Times Cooking: No-Recipe Recipes is a cookbook by Sam Sifton, the founding editor of New York Times Cooking. It describes dishes through loose guidelines instead of exact measurements, encouraging home cooks to improvise with what they have on hand.
B320: A Recipe for Bees is a novel by the Canadian author Gail Anderson-Dargatz. It follows Augusta Olsen, a woman in her seventies who reflects on her long marriage and her family history while keeping bees on a farm in British Columbia.
B021: Accordion Crimes is a 1996 novel by E. Annie Proulx. It follows a single green accordion as it passes between owners across a century of American life, tracing immigrant communities from Sicilians and Germans to Mexicans and Cajuns.
B035: Catch-22 is Joseph Heller's 1961 satirical novel set among a US Army Air Forces bomber squadron in Italy during the Second World War. Captain John Yossarian tries to survive his required missions while military bureaucracy keeps raising the number, and the paradox of the title governs his options.
B078: Der Coup von Berdac appears to be a German-language novel attributed to Michael Roes, a German writer known for fiction, essays, and film work. The edition could not be confirmed with certainty, so the description stays general.
B005: Habitus is a 2004 novel by the British writer James Flint. Its story of a man pursuing a lost love moves through cultures and cities, with themes of technology, nomadic living, and the shifting relationship between people and the places they inhabit.
B132: High Fidelity is Nick Hornby's 1995 novel about Rob Fleming, the owner of a failing record shop in north London. After his girlfriend leaves, Rob revisits his past relationships and ranks them in the same way he compiles his lists of favorite albums.
B256: Jim the Boy is a 2000 novel by Tony Earley, set in rural North Carolina in the 1930s. It follows Jim Glass, a boy of 10 raised by his widowed mother and three uncles, through a year of small-town childhood.
B193: Mao II is a 1991 novel by Don DeLillo about Bill Gray, a reclusive American novelist who has withdrawn from public life. His decision to be photographed draws him toward a hostage crisis in Beirut, and the book explores crowds, terrorism, and the place of the writer in modern culture.
B027: Shampoo Planet is a 1992 novel by the Canadian writer Douglas Coupland. Its narrator, Tyler Johnson, is a young man in Lancaster, California, who cares about style and travels to Europe, and the story follows his relationships with his bohemian mother and his friends.
B054: The Bedroom Secrets of the Master Chefs is a 2006 novel by the Scottish author Irvine Welsh. Set in Edinburgh and told largely in dialect, it follows a food inspector, a bitter chef, and a young woman whose lives intersect around an inheritance, with Welsh's usual dark comedy.
B312: The Innocent is a 1990 novel by Ian McEwan, set in Berlin during the early Cold War. A young British technician, Leonard Marnham, is assigned to a joint Anglo-American project to tap Soviet communications, and he becomes entangled in a relationship that ends in violence.
B319: The Master and Margarita is a novel by the Russian writer Mikhail Bulgakov, written in the 1930s and first published in the 1960s. The devil arrives in Soviet Moscow with a retinue that disrupts the literary establishment, while a parallel narrative retells the story of Pontius Pilate.
B119: The Secret Agent is a 1907 novel by Joseph Conrad, set in London in the 1880s. It follows Adolf Verloc, a shopkeeper who also works as a spy and provocateur, whose assignment to provoke an anarchist outrage leads to a bombing at the Greenwich Observatory.
B060: The Time Traveler's Wife is a 2003 debut novel by Audrey Niffenegger. It tells the story of Henry DeTamble, who has a genetic disorder that moves him unpredictably through time, and Clare Abshire, who meets him at different ages throughout her life in Chicago.
B133: White Teeth is Zadie Smith's 2000 debut novel, set in north London. It follows the families of Archie Jones, an Englishman, and Samad Iqbal, a Bangladeshi immigrant, across several decades, covering friendship, immigration, religion, and the conflicts between generations.
B170: Bleeding Hearts is a 1994 thriller by the Scottish writer Ian Rankin, published under the pseudonym Jack Harvey. Its plot follows Michael Doyle, an assassin hired for a job in the United States, whose assignment is complicated by an FBI agent and a woman from his past.
B318: Country of the Blind is the 1997 debut novel by the Scottish writer Christopher Brookmyre. Set in Scotland, it combines a political murder, a dark comic plot, and a reporter investigating the death of a Tory MP at a country house gathering.
B103: Der Sommermörder is the German edition of Beneath the Skin, the 1997 psychological thriller by Nicci French, the joint pen name of Nicci Gerrard and Sean French. Three women in London receive threatening letters from a man who then begins to attack them.
B308: Firewall is a 1998 novel by the Swedish author Henning Mankell and the eighth Kurt Wallander mystery. When a man dies of a heart attack at a cash machine in Ystad, Wallander investigates and finds a link to a plot against the country's financial systems.
B117: Inferno is a 2013 thriller by Dan Brown and the fourth novel featuring Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon. Langdon wakes in a Florence hospital with memory loss and follows clues drawn from Dante's Divine Comedy while pursued by agents tied to a genetic engineer.
B143: Never End is a Gothenburg-set crime novel by the Swedish author Åke Edwardson, first published in Swedish in 2000 and translated into English by Laurie Thompson. Chief Inspector Erik Winter investigates the murder of a young woman in a park, which echoes an unsolved case from years earlier.
B263: Reamde is a 2011 thriller by Neal Stephenson. A ransomware attack on a popular online fantasy game draws in a game company founder, his niece, and a group of criminals and jihadists, and the plot travels from North America to China and beyond.
B139: Skinny Dip is a 2004 comic crime novel by Carl Hiaasen, set in Florida. After a man throws his wife off a cruise ship, she survives, and she conspires with an eccentric former police officer to unsettle him while he is involved in a scheme polluting the Everglades.
B309: Tears of the Giraffe is the second novel in Alexander McCall Smith's No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency series, set in Botswana. Precious Ramotswe takes on a case concerning an American mother whose son vanished a decade earlier, while her domestic life changes at home in Gaborone.
B046: The Devil's Feather is a 2005 crime novel by the British writer Minette Walters. Journalist Connie Burns, investigating a series of murders linked to a mercenary in Sierra Leone, finds he has followed her to England, and the story moves between West Africa and a quiet English village.
B255: The Get is a crime novel by the Canadian author Dietrich Kalteis, published by ECW Press. It follows criminals and the people around them in a violent story of money, loyalty, and betrayal, in the author's usual period crime style.
B224: The Impossible Fortune is the fifth novel in Richard Osman's Thursday Murder Club series. The retirees of Coopers Chase, a village for older residents in Kent, take on another case as Elizabeth, Joyce, Ibrahim, and Ron examine a link to a missing fortune.
B271: The Snowman is a 2007 crime novel by the Norwegian author Jo Nesbø, the seventh book to feature Oslo detective Harry Hole. Hole investigates a series of disappearances of married women that coincide with the first snowfall, and he suspects a killer who leaves snowmen at the scenes.
B313: All Tomorrow's Parties is a 1999 science fiction novel by William Gibson and the third book in his Bridge trilogy. Set in a near-future San Francisco, it follows characters including Colin Laney, who sees patterns in data, as events converge on a coming cultural shift.
B310: Feersum Endjinn is a 1994 science fiction novel by Iain M. Banks that stands apart from his Culture series. It is set in a far-future castle on a dying Earth, and one of its narrators is written in phonetic spelling.
B305: Pollen is a 1995 science fiction novel by the British author Jeff Noon, set in the Manchester of the Vurt universe. A detective investigates a death linked to a plague of pollen, and the novel combines drugs, feathers, and dream-like technology in a surreal near future.
B113: The Hydrogen Sonata is a 2012 novel by Iain M. Banks and the tenth Culture novel. It is set around the Gzilt civilization, whose members prepare to Sublime, and a plot about a secret in the Gzilt's past draws in the Culture's warships and minds.
B314: A Dirty Job is a 2006 comic fantasy by Christopher Moore, set in San Francisco. Charlie Asher, a beta male who runs a secondhand shop, becomes a Death Merchant who collects the souls of the dying, which leaves him managing his infant daughter alongside his new duties.
B265: Heroes is a 2018 retelling of Greek myths by Stephen Fry, the second volume after Mythos. It covers the tales of Perseus, Heracles, Jason, Atalanta, Theseus, and other mortal figures, written in an informal narrative voice with commentary on the sources.
B094: Schattenschwester is the German title of The Shadow Sister, the third novel in Lucinda Riley's Seven Sisters series, and the attribution to Peter Straub appears incorrect. Star D'Aplièse, one of six adopted sisters, follows clues about her origins to London and traces a connection to the early twentieth century.
B232: The Lord of the Rings is J. R. R. Tolkien's high fantasy epic, published in three volumes in 1954 and 1955. Frodo Baggins and a fellowship set out to destroy the One Ring in Mordor, in a conflict that shapes the future of Middle-earth.
B039: Unseen Academicals is a 2009 Discworld novel by Terry Pratchett. It follows the wizards of Unseen University as they revive the old street game of football in Ankh-Morpork, while Mr. Nutt, a candle dribbler, and a cook named Juliet become involved.
B014: Baudolino is a 2000 historical novel by the Italian writer Umberto Eco, set in the twelfth century. The title character, a peasant who becomes an adopted son of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, tells his life story to a Byzantine historian, with travels to the mythical kingdom of Prester John.
B316: Conspiracy is a 2013 historical mystery by S. J. Parris and the third novel featuring Giordano Bruno. Set in Elizabethan England in 1585, the former friar works as a spy for Francis Walsingham and investigates a plot to place Mary, Queen of Scots on the throne.
B236: Fall of Giants is a 2010 historical novel by Ken Follett and the first volume of the Century Trilogy. It follows five interconnected families in the United States, Britain, Germany, Russia, and Wales through the First World War and the Russian Revolution.
B070: Montenegro is a historical novel by Starling Lawrence, an American editor and writer. Its story reaches from the Balkans into wider Europe in the early twentieth century, following a young protagonist through a period of political and personal upheaval.
B167: The Radetzky March is a 1932 novel by the Austrian author Joseph Roth. It follows three generations of the Trotta family, whose fortunes are tied to the Habsburg monarchy, from the battle of Solferino to the empire's collapse after the First World War.
B225: Can Holding In a Fart Kill You? is a humor and science book by Andrew Thompson that answers odd questions about the body and daily life. Its short entries cover topics from digestion to household curiosities and use a conversational explanatory approach.
B019: Loriots heile Welt is a German-language collection of cartoons and sketches by Loriot, the stage name of the German humorist Vicco von Bülow. It gathers his drawings and comic scenes depicting bourgeois life, awkward conversations, and the small mishaps of German everyday life.
B296: My Neighbor Totoro, Vol. 1 is the first volume of the manga adaptation of the 1988 animated film by Hayao Miyazaki. Two sisters, Satsuki and Mei, move to the countryside in postwar Japan while their mother recovers in hospital, and they meet forest spirits including Totoro.
B162: The Little Prince is a novella by the French writer and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, first published in 1943. A pilot stranded in the Sahara meets a young prince from a small asteroid, who recounts his travels to other planets and his love for a rose.
B303: Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World is a 1997 book by Mark Kurlansky. It traces the history of the North Atlantic cod fishery and its role in European and American economies, from Viking voyages to modern collapse, and includes recipes from different periods.
B114: London: The Biography is a 2000 history by Peter Ackroyd. Organized by theme and without a strict chronology, it follows the city from its prehistoric origins to the present, covering its streets, trades, crime, plague, fire, and the habits of its inhabitants.
B267: SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome is a 2015 book by the classicist Mary Beard. It covers roughly a thousand years, from the early city to the citizenship edict of 212 CE, and examines how Rome grew from a small settlement into an empire.
B270: Wayward Lives, Beautiful Experiments is a 2019 history by the scholar Saidiya Hartman. Drawing on archives, it recounts the lives of young Black women in early twentieth-century Philadelphia and New York, and it describes their search for freedom and intimacy in urban life.
B278: A Tour on the Prairies is a travel narrative by Washington Irving, published in 1835. Irving describes a month-long journey in 1832 through what is now Oklahoma with a party of rangers, with accounts of buffalo hunts, camp life, and encounters with the landscape.
B190: Dispatches from Pluto is a 2015 travel memoir by the British writer Richard Grant. After moving to the Mississippi Delta with his girlfriend, he describes the region's people, history, food, and customs, and the problems of settling in a place he finds both foreign and welcoming.
B116: The Hotel Years is a collection of travel journalism by the Austrian writer Joseph Roth, drawn from his newspaper work between the wars. His pieces describe cities and rail journeys across Europe, written in the 1920s and 1930s while he lived in hotels, and they capture a continent in transition.
B325: Far Out Isn't Far Enough is a memoir by the Alsatian-born illustrator Tomi Ungerer. It covers his childhood under Nazi occupation, his work as a children's author and satirical artist in New York, and his later life in Nova Scotia and Ireland.
B273: Me is the 2019 autobiography of Elton John, the British singer and songwriter. He describes his childhood in Pinner, his rise to fame in the 1970s, his songwriting partnership with Bernie Taupin, his struggles with addiction, and his later work as an advocate and father.
B123: Clean Meat is a 2018 book by Paul Shapiro, an animal protection advocate. It reports on the development of meat grown from animal cells, profiling the scientists and entrepreneurs involved and discussing the technology's prospects for food production, the environment, and animal welfare.
B045: The World Without Us is a 2007 book by the journalist Alan Weisman. It imagines how the planet would change if humans vanished, describing how buildings, infrastructure, and ecosystems would decay or recover, and what traces of civilization might remain for millennia.
B154: Spent: Sex, Evolution, and Consumer Behavior is a 2009 book by the evolutionary psychologist Geoffrey Miller. It argues that consumer choices work largely as displays of traits such as intelligence, conscientiousness, and agreeableness, and it applies evolutionary theory to marketing and shopping.
B223: The Future of Truth is a 2019 book by the German filmmaker Werner Herzog, translated into English. Herzog reflects on truth, fabrication, and the ways images and information shape belief, drawing on examples from his films, travels, and encounters across several decades.
B269: Good to Great is a 2001 business book by Jim Collins. His research team studied 11 companies that sustained strong stock performance after a period of average results, and the book identifies common practices such as disciplined people, disciplined thought, and disciplined action.
B288: Reinvention is a business book by Arlene Dickinson, the Canadian entrepreneur and former Dragons' Den investor. It draws on her own career setbacks and her experience advising companies, and it lays out steps for changing course in work and business.
B001: Winning is a 2005 management book by Jack Welch, the former chairman of General Electric, written with his wife Suzy Welch. It offers advice on leadership, hiring, strategy, and career decisions, and it uses a question and answer format along with anecdotes from his time at GE.
B164: Design of the 20th Century is a large illustrated survey by Charlotte and Peter Fiell, published by Taschen. It presents furniture, products, and graphics from the century's major designers and movements, organized by period with short texts and reference material.
B287: Keep Out! Build Your Own Backyard Clubhouse is a project book by Lee Mothes. It gives plans and step-by-step directions for building small playhouses and hideouts, with materials lists, tool advice, and designs for a range of skill levels.
